title: Bank of America Returns its “Golf with Us” Program for a Second Year
description: Bank of America’s “Golf with Us” program offers 150,000 free, year-long memberships to the nonprofit organization Youth on Course.   Bank of America announced the return of its “Golf with Us” program via a press release on April 8, bringing back the initiative after a strong inaugural year. In the program’s first year, it drew close to 100,000 participants a[...]
text:
Photo courtesy of Bank of America
Bank of America’s “Golf with Us” program offers 150,000 free, year-long memberships to the nonprofit organization Youth on Course.
 
Bank of America announced the return of its “Golf with Us” program via a press release on April 8, bringing back the initiative after a strong inaugural year.
In the program’s first year, it drew close to 100,000 participants across the United States and Puerto Rico, according to the press release. This year the company hopes to enroll 150,000. 
“Our belief in the power of sport to bring people together and broaden opportunity is reinforced by our partnerships that help us build stronger client connections, support local economies and inspire future generations,” Chair and CEO of Bank of America Brian Moynihan said in the press release. “In its first year, Golf with Us has helped nearly 100,000 kids learn invaluable life skills, and we look forward to building on this momentum with Rory’s terrific support and partners like Youth on Course.”
The Rory Moynihan referred to is now two-time Masters champion, Rory McIlroy. Bank of America is a “Champion Partner” of the Masters Tournament and debuted a marketing campaign recreating iconic Masters moments — including moments from McIlroy’s Masters victory last year — with “Golf with Us” participants acting as the athletes. The campaign inspired McIlroy to donate $500,000 to Youth on Course, according to the press release. 
“I remember being a kid trying to copy everything the players I looked up to did, the swing, the mannerisms, all of it. The idea of a young kid recreating that shot on 15 really resonated with me,” McIlroy said via the press release. “Golf teaches powerful life lessons, how to compete, stay patient, and handle setbacks, and those lessons shape who you become. Opening access to the game is key to giving more kids that opportunity.”
Bank of America’s “Golf with Us” program is open to all children between the ages of six and 18. Those enrolled in the program will have access to multiple benefits including $5 tee times, complimentary access to GolfPass and a registered handicap index with the United States Golf Association’s Golf Handicap Information Network system, according to the press release. New this year, benefits will also include $5 simulator rentals and a free lesson from a PGA pro at any Golf Galaxy or Dick’s House of Sport location.  
There are six courses in Delaware accessible through the “Golf with Us” program including: Delcastle Golf Course, American Classic Golf Course, Eagle Creek Golf Course, Garrisons Lake Golf Club, Jonathan’s Landing Golf Club and Mulligan’s Pointe. There are three locations offering $5 simulator rentals. Those are the Golf Galaxy stores in Christiana and Newark and the Dick’s House of Sport located in Wilmington.
“At Bank of America, we see ‘Golf with Us’ as a vital investment in the future of our young people right here in Delaware. It’s about breaking down barriers and making golf truly accessible and affordable for the next generation,” President of Bank of America Delaware Kelly Firment, said in a press release.  
The “Golf with Us” program is open to the first 150,000 new participants that enroll in the program before June 15. Participants can sign up using this link. Returning members are eligible for a 20 percent discount when renewing their annual Youth on Course membership, according to the press release.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Amid ‘nuclear renaissance,’ Idaho worries about job demands coming to the Intermountain West
description: As Utah takes action to power up its nuclear ambitions, the next generation of workers needed for future reactors are mostly unprepared. In neighboring Idaho, which hosts the Idaho National Lab focused on nuclear research, the scenario is similar and keeps some state officials up at night trying to find solutions for what’s expected to […]
text:
(Illustration by Alex Cochran for Utah News Dispatch)As Utah takes action to power up its nuclear ambitions, the next generation of workers needed for future reactors are mostly unprepared. In neighboring Idaho, which hosts the Idaho National Lab focused on nuclear research, the scenario is similar and keeps some state officials up at night trying to find solutions for what’s expected to become a booming workforce market. 
Wendi Secrist, executive director at the Idaho Workforce Development Council, says her office keeps busy trying to figure out ways to grow the workforce to meet the needs of the nuclear energy industry amid its comeback propelled by the Trump administration. 
If the U.S. Department of Energy wants to accomplish its goal to produce 400 gigawatts of nuclear energy by 2050, it’s going to need an additional 184,000 people in the nuclear industry, and that doesn’t include the additional 250,000 workers needed for construction, Secrist said, referencing a 2025 workforce study commissioned by the Department of Energy.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
“We need to start thinking about how are we going to build this, how many of those (184,000) jobs collectively should we be looking at being located here in the Intermountain West and preparing for,” Secrist said during the 2026 John Horan Health Physics Symposium the University of Utah hosted on Friday.
With nuclear projects coming to Utah, Cox hopes for rural jobs, but that’s no easy task

The same question has concerned Utah leaders as well. Gov. Spencer Cox said at a September energy conference that the recruiting challenges experienced by the industry so far are “terrifying.” He, however, remained hopeful about what the new openings would mean for communities in rural Utah and argued that incorporating work earlier into education may help ease that burden.
While states in the region could certainly look at the available projections, Secrist said, the best way to figure out how to respond to the coming boom in demand is to maintain discussions with nuclear companies about their expectations — but also their realities.
“Are they expecting that they’re going to hire an engineer with 12 years of experience? Well, that might be what they put on the job description. But what are they really doing? Because what does the market have available for them?” she said. “And so being able to take all of that information in and start building out a workforce plan is what we have to do.” 
Utah has been laying the foundation to allocate more funds to energy jobs that are considered in high demand, but has also announced plans to build a nuclear “energy ecosystem” in Brigham City, which is expected to include a workforce training center. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Following a nationwide trend of decreasing birthrates, even in Utah, the Idaho Workforce Development Council is also thinking about how to work with fewer people entering the workforce, Secrist said.
“It’s not going to just work itself out. We have to be intentional. We have to be thinking about not only are we building the right programs, but are we getting people into the right programs?” she said. “So we have to be really, really efficient with the people that we have, and we have to be thinking about how are we going to attract more people.”
In Idaho, for example, there have been some initiatives led by the national lab to create nuclear trades programs and a nuclear technology associate’s degree, with “a lot of outreach,”  Secrist said.
Idaho is also looking to make nuclear industry jobs exciting for students earlier in their academic trajectories with initiatives meant to create gateways for those encountering challenges in STEM programs, she said. Like in Utah, the hope is that rural communities begin a nuclear workforce culture.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Legislature 2026: A ‘get in, get out’ session that wasn’t
description: Alabama lawmakers used all 30 days for the 2026 legislative session, an unusual and unexpected move for an election year given leadership’s previously stated priority of “get in and get out.” Election year sessions tend to focus on budgets. But this year, lawmakers found themselves addressing — often unwillingly — many other issues during their […]
text:
A group of senators and personnel gathered around a lectern on the floor of the Alabama Senate on April 7, 2026. Clockwise, left to right: Sen. Vivian Davis Figures, D-Mobile; Jess Skaggs, chief of staff for Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger; Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur; Sen. Jack Williams, R-Wilmer; Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman and Sen. Gerald Allen, R-Cottondale. Going into the 2026 legislative session, Gudger said the goal was to "get in and get out" so lawmakers could campaign. But, the legislative body used all 30 days available to them, and did not finish work on the state's budgets until the 29th day. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)Alabama lawmakers used all 30 days for the 2026 legislative session, an unusual and unexpected move for an election year given leadership’s previously stated priority of “get in and get out.”
Election year sessions tend to focus on budgets. But this year, lawmakers found themselves addressing — often unwillingly — many other issues during their 86 calendar days on Goat Hill, including attempts to reform the state’s public utility regulation board amid rising complaints over Alabama’s region-leading power bills, and Alabama Republican Party-pushed legislation that would have closed the state’s primary elections. 
Impressions of the session divided on party lines. Democrats criticized the Republican majority for focusing on legislation mainly popular with GOP activists. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
“We cut our nose off to spite our face here in Alabama,” said Rep. Marilyn Lands, D-Huntsville. “We could have expanded Medicaid, we could have the lottery, we could do more for voting rights. We do a lot of things that don’t even make sense to me. They’re renaming the Gulf of [Mexico], all these bills about school prayer and the Ten Commandments and abstinence based sex education that’s not what the people want.”
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, said the session was “rough.” 
“It’s an election year, and you get a lot of different bills coming from different places that you think that people just want to do it for headlines because of reelection packages, but, we’ve seen some bills that we think that really kind of hurt people,” Singleton said in an interview Wednesday. 
Republicans pointed to the relatively easy passage of budgets and what Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, said was a “pretty smooth” three months in the Senate.
“To the point where some people said, ‘Hey, you’re starting to get boring up there. You’re not debating as much and having some fireworks,’” Gudger said Thursday. “I think it’s because of communication up and down the hallway before we came to the floor.”
Sen. Chris Elliott, R-Josephine, said the session was the best he’s been a part of since his first in 2019. 
“The magnitude and quality of legislation that we’ve passed, the demeanor on the floor, the management of the flow of work has been just impressive,” he said in an interview Thursday. 
The Senate did not experience anything like the end of the 2025 session, which ended in a filibuster and a backlog of local bills, until the very last day, when the dispute over the closed primary bill doomed several pieces of legislation. 
Sen. Rodger Smitherman, D-Birmingham, said in an interview after adjournment on Thursday that this was the first year he felt the whole chamber worked together. 
“This time, we started and we had conversations and said ‘how can we find ways to pull in the same direction?’ We did that from the beginning,” Smitherman said. “As we moved through, I think the pinnacle of how far we came was the one day they did the clotures. Then, we got back up and said come on now. And then they went right back and made a whole new calendar and the whole calendar was all our bills.”
PSC fight
Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, speaking to Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth on the floor of the Alabama Senate on March 12, 2026, in the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Gudger said in an interview after sine die adjournment Thursday that HB 475, sponsored by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, was the most stressful bill the Legislature considered. 
The law prohibits the Public Service Commission (PSC) from increasing electricity rates until 2029. As originally filed, HB 475 would have required the PSC to hold formal rate case hearings every three years, requiring sworn testimony from utility officials to justify proposed rate increases. 
Alabama has not had a formal rate case hearing since 1981, and the state now faces some of the highest electricity rates in the South. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Georgia’s average residential energy prices in January were 14.46 cents per kW/hr in January, compared to 16.06 cents per kW/hr in Alabama.
However, the Senate radically altered the bill, removing the formal hearing requirement and changing the structure of the PSC from a president and two commissioners to seven members, one from each of the state’s seven congressional districts, whose elections will be phased in through 2030. Gov. Kay Ivey will appoint four members by July 15, from a list of nominees submitted by legislative leaders. In addition, the bill creates a secretary of energy, to be appointed by the next governor, who would administer the PSC and have significant power over it. 
Sen. Clyde Chambliss, R-Prattville, who introduced the changes to the bill, said the PSC “had a problem” in an interview on Wednesday, and that “time will tell” if the bill works. 
“If we missed the mark a little bit, we’ll come back and address it again,” he said.
Butler did not vote for the altered version of his bill. Critics said the changes could pack the PSC with pro-utility commissioners and effectively mute the voice of the public in the process. Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, a renewable energy advocacy group that strongly criticized the legislation, said in a statement that the legislation was “effectively handing a political appointee a veto over your electric bill.” 
“Completely rewriting a bill and passing it through the entire Senate in less than 48 hours is not consumer protection,” the statement said. “It’s Alabama Power protection.”
Gudger said he believed the bill “will reduce electrical rates for people throughout the state, whether you’re a single mom or elderly people or small businesses.”
“I do think it was a huge lift restructuring the PSC, and that’ll be something that will last, I believe, 75 to 100 years,” he said.
Ivey signed HB 475 into law on April 2. It goes into effect on June 1, and she will make her appointments no later than July 15. 
Primary fights
Rep. Ernie Yarbrough, R-Trinity, speaks on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on March 19, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
About midway through the session, the Alabama Republican Party made statewide party registration – something Alabama has never had — its top legislative priority, arguing it was needed to ensure candidates represented their party. 
HB 541, sponsored by Rep. Ernie Yarbrough, R-Trinity, was unusually controversial for a GOP-backed bill. The House passed the legislation in March, but several Republican members of the legislature were sharply critical of the legislation, saying it could drive away independent voters. Rep. Chris Pringle, R-Mobile, voted for the bill but not before calling it “arrogance beyond all comprehension.”
The Senate was also divided on the measure. HB 541 was on Thursday’s agenda, but Sen. David Sessions, R-Grand Bay, said he planned to offer a substitute to the legislation. Gudger said the party pushed the bill on them. Ledbetter said Thursday after the House’s final adjournment that he wished the bill had passed.
“We passed the closed primaries bill and I thought it was a good bill. Why it waited so long, I don’t know,” he said. “I suspect it’ll come back and so we’ll see how that goes.”
Budgets
Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, stands on the floor of the Alabama Senate on March 5, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Lawmakers did not complete work on the budgets until Wednesday, the 29th day of the session. Both budgets reflected the loss of federal COVID dollars and uncertainties about the state economy in the coming year.
The Legislature passed a $10.5 billion Education Trust Fund Budget that included a 2% teacher pay raise and increased funding for the CHOOSE Act, the state’s school voucher program, but saw other programs such as Alabama Reading Initiative remain level-funded. 
The budget also included funding for the Public Education Employees’ Health Insurance Plan (PEEHIP) at a $1,048 per member per month rate, leaving the rest of the funding to the PEEHIP board to meet rising health care costs.
Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, chair of the Senate Finance and Taxation Education Committee, said in an interview Thursday that he is “very pleased” with another record breaking ETF.
“With the pay raise for educators and the bonus for retirees and being able to keep both parties’ health insurance premiums flat, so they won’t see additional costs on the health care side of things,” he said. “That was a real challenge.”
The $3.7 billion General Fund budget  is an $8.1 million (0.2%) increase over the current year’s budget, and about $49 million more than Ivey’s recommendation. The relatively small increase reflects concerns about state revenues over the coming year, with several state agencies getting the same allocations they are budgeted to receive this year.  
Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, chair of the Senate Finance and Taxation General Fund Committee, said in an interview Thursday that both budgets are “good.”
“Even though they’re spending large sums that we’re unaccustomed to in our history, I think we’ve handled it very well, and we’re doing it in a great way.”
The Alabama Medicaid Agency is level-funded at $1.18 billion for the year. There are about 1.1 million Alabamians enrolled in Medicaid, about half of whom are children. The Department of Corrections will receive $868 million for the year, about $500,000 more than the current year’s budget. 
Corrections and Medicaid receive most of the money from the General Fund budget. 
The budget also includes $16 million for a 2% pay raise for state employees and $18 million for the State Employees Insurance Board to offset the rising healthcare costs. 
Currently, the state pays $1,025 per member per month, but due to rising health costs, CEO of the State Employees Insurance Board (SEIB) in September requested a $150 increase per member per month. Lawmakers had expressed doubts about their ability to honor that request, but were able to in the final version.
Ivey signed the budgets on Thursday.
Other notable bills
Sen. Donnie Chesteen, R-Geneva, sitting at his desk on the floor of the Alabama Senate on Feb. 26, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
SB 71, a controversial bill that could weaken the state’s environmental regulations sponsored by Sen. Donnie Chesteen, R-Geneva, would prohibit Alabama from having stricter environmental regulations than the federal government. The bill moved quickly through both chambers sparking concerns from Democrats and environmentalists in the state who said the bill could leave Alabamians more susceptible to pollution and unsafe environmental conditions. The law went into effect immediately. 
HB 41, sponsored by Rep. Matt Simpson, R-Daphne, expands the death penalty to include rape, sodomy and sexual torture of a minor under 12 years old. The bill passed after House Democrats raised concerns about retraumatizing victims and violating a 2008 U.S. Supreme Court ruling. This was the second year the legislation was introduced and Simpson cited a Bibb County sex trafficking ring as reasoning for bringing the bill again. The law goes into effect Oct. 1. 
HB 517, sponsored by Rep. James Lomax, R-Huntsville, establishes the Talent Readiness and Industry Needs (TRAIN) Act to allow businesses to collaborate with educational institutions to provide career and technical education training. If signed, it will go into effect Oct. 1. 
HB 520, sponsored by Rep. Marcus Paramore, R-Troy, requires the State Board of Education to create an expedited certification pathway for teachers to be able to teach career and technical education courses. If signed, it would go into effect June 1.
Ledbetter said on Thursday more Career and Technical Education bills can be expected in the future.
“In the last two years, we put $250 million to expand and grow career tech facilities because we’ve got to catch up,” he said. “We’ve got 138 school districts and only 80 career tech facilities. And then 66% of our kids aren’t going to college, so I think we’ve got to fill that gap.”
HB 300, sponsored by Rep. Frances Holk-Jones, R-Foley, requires health insurers to pay for or reimburse beneficiaries for breast cancer screenings and any subsequent tests. The law goes into effect on Jan. 1. Another cancer screening bill, SB 19, sponsored by Senate Majority Leader Steve Livingston, R-Scottsboro, allows all men over 50 and high risk men over 40 to be screened for prostate cancer without any cost-sharing obligations. The law goes into effect on Oct. 1, 2027. 
HB 86, sponsored by Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, requires the Alabama Board of Pardons and Paroles to consider educational and employment achievements by parole applicants while incarcerated. The law goes into effect on Oct. 1. SB 240, sponsored by Sen. Will Barfoot, R-Pike Road, allows victims of crimes and parole applicants to attend parole hearings virtually. The law goes into effect on March 1.
What didn’t pass
Rep. Adline Clarke, D-Mobile, speaks on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on Feb. 5, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
HB 13, sponsored by Rep. Ernie Yarbrough, R-Trinity, would have allowed local law enforcement to collaborate with federal agencies to enforce immigration laws. It’s unclear how the legislation would have differed from 287(g) programs which already allow the collaborations to take place. The bill failed to pass the Senate Thursday after the House adjourned sine die causing all business in the upper chamber to grind to a halt. 
HB 363, sponsored by Rep. Greg Barnes, R-Curry, would have banned interrupting a worship service by engaging in unlawful protests, riots or disorderly conduct. After passing the House in February, the bill failed to get a final vote in the Senate because the House adjourned sine die.
HB 486, sponsored by Rep. Adline Clarke, D-Mobile, would have automatically restored voting rights to individuals convicted of felony offences; allow for no-excuse absentee voting; let people vote prior to Election Day and create an Alabama Voting Rights Commission to review rules changes for voting and preclear actions related to voting related to voting that could discriminate against protected classes of voters. The bill was approved by the House Judiciary Committee with just three days left in the session and failed to make it to the House calendar for a full vote.
Clarke said Thursday that while the bill never got a full vote, she was pleased that it at least got out of committee.
“We brought that bill forth on last year and it got no movement whatsoever so we were just pleased that we were able to get a favorable report on the Alabama Voting Rights Commission Bill on this particular session and hope that we can advance it, and get it across the finish line next session,” she said.
HB 50, sponsored by Rep. Terri Collins, R-Decatur, would have permanently funded the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, the legislation would have codified an executive order Ivey signed in 2023. The bill passed the House, but failed to make it to the Senate floor for a full vote.
“It’s my third year, and it’s not passed so it won’t pass while I’m here,” Collins said Thursday afternoon.
SB 298, sponsored by Sen. Will Barfoot, R-Pike Road, would have required cities, Montgomery in particular, to maintain a ratio of 1.9 to 1,000 law enforcement officers to residents or have the state oversee their departments. The bill drew sharp criticism from Montgomery Police Chief James Graboys, local clergy and Sen. Kirk Hatcher, D-Montgomery, who represents most of the city.
The bill was the only one on the House’s final agenda that was not voted on due to Ledbetter’s prediction of a filibuster.
No gambling legislation 
Rep. Juandalynn Givan, D-Birmingham (center) speaks with Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on April 8, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. Behind Givan is Rep. Chris Blackshear, R-Smiths Station. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
After a divisive battle over a comprehensive gambling bill in 2024, legislative leaders have shown no appetite for legislation establishing a lottery or settling the legal status of wagering in the state. No gambling bill got serious consideration in the 2026 session. Rep. Juandalynn Givan, D-Birmingham, said Thursday that meant the session was incomplete.  
“Every four years, we come back to this place, and we say we’re going to allow their voices to be heard,” she said.”That answer has never been laid on the table to a question that has been asked over and over.”
A new beginning
The 2026 legislative session was the last in the current Statehouse, barring any special sessions, until it moves into a new building. Lawmakers were ready to leave the current building Thursday afternoon.
The current Statehouse, which has long suffered mold and structural issues, will be vacated this summer. Staff and lawmakers will move into the new Statehouse under construction nearby. After the move, the building will be demolished.
Orr said the current building is a “fire trap.” There are two accessible stairwells in the building, but they are on opposite sides of the building. Legislators, staff and visitors are concentrated on one side of the building on floors five through eight. 
“Today on the stairwell, three or four times already there were school children going up seven, eight flights of stairs. People, staffers, senators, representatives, trying to go the opposite direction, with the totally congested stairwells,” he said. “If we had a fire, what a mess this building is. A fire trap, if we had an emergency evacuation situation.”
Collins, who isn’t seeking re-election, said she wasn’t upset over the building being demolished soon but that she had fond memories in the current State House.
Construction workers walk across the rotunda of the new Alabama Statehouse on Jan. 29, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. Work on the building, the first new statehouse in the United States since 1977, is expected to be completed this summer. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
“The memories are that you can’t breathe and you’re all sick at the end of the year because all of the walls are full of mold, so I’m not going to be really sad it’s torn down, it’s needed to be for a while,” she said. “I’ve had great meetings, I’ve had contentious meetings, [but] I have wonderful memories from every floor.”
Clarke said she wasn’t feeling sentimental being in the current State House on its assumed final day. 
“I’m more concerned about representing and helping to improve the quality of life for all Alabamians whether it’s in this old building or in a new one,” she said.
The Legislature will return, but in its new home on Ripley Street and at least nine new lawmakers, in February.

name: Nevada Current
title: Democratic candidate for governor slams data center tax breaks
description: As the rapid rollout of data centers across Nevada creates tensions between municipal governments and residents, Democratic gubernatorial candidates are tapping into voter discontent with the status quo.  In small towns across Nevada, residents are accusing local representatives of pushing development through without public input or proper examination of pot[...]
text:
Democratic candidate for governor Alexis Hill speaking in Boulder City on April 9, 2026. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)As the rapid rollout of data centers across Nevada creates tensions between municipal governments and residents, Democratic gubernatorial candidates are tapping into voter discontent with the status quo. 
In small towns across Nevada, residents are accusing local representatives of pushing development through without public input or proper examination of potential impacts to local residents.
A proposed data center in Boulder City’s El Dorado Valley is the latest example of that conflict, resulting in a deepening distrust of local government and a push for statewide policies to address the skyrocketing demand for data centers.
There are currently no state or county-wide regulations in Nevada guiding where data centers can and can’t be built, forcing regional planners to develop long-term plans for land use on the fly.
Last week, Democratic candidate for governor Alexis Hill hosted a packed data center town hall in Boulder City, where residents have protested plans to build a 88.5-acre data center about three miles southwest of the town.
The development proposed by Townsite Solar 2 LLC, an affiliate of Houston-based Skylar Energy Management, was awarded property and sales tax abatements by the Nevada Governor’s Office of Energy in 2024.
Under that agreement, the data center is expected to operate for at least 10 years and will receive more than $24.3 million in tax abatements. 
The proposed Boulder City data center is not the only one to receive generous tax abatements. Over fiscal years 2023 and 2024, property tax breaks provided to data centers totaled $13.3 million, and sales and use tax breaks totaled $225.6 million, according to the Nevada Department of Taxation.
During the town hall last week Hill, who has been critical of the state’s policy of giving tax breaks to new or expanding companies, outlined her plan to address regional impacts of data centers through executive orders, including freezing new tax abatements and reviewing the impact of existing data center operations on water use and energy prices.
“I want to get rid of these abatements immediately by executive order. The governor can do that right now,” said Hill. “Nevadans have already spent millions in taxpayer funds to incentivize an industry that does not need handouts.”
During the town hall, Boulder City residents raised concerns about the amount of energy and water the data center is expected to use. According to an application, the data center will use a hybrid closed-loop cooling system that would use both water and air cooling. 
The data center could use as much as 650,000 gallons of water a day, according to the application, which also notes that when air cooling is being used the data center would require up to 25% more power. Residents stressed their concerns that higher energy use by the industrial data center could significantly increase their utility bills.
Hill, who is a Washoe County Commissioner, said Nevada needs to establish a state permitting process to ensure local jurisdictions have proper guidance on regulating data centers.
“We have no guidance right now from the state on how data centers can be permitted, and local governments are trying their best to regulate, including water authorities as well. And we are not in the best position to do that without guidance from the state,” Hill said. 
Ford, who released his own energy outline earlier this month, has proposed requiring data centers “commit to paying for the energy they consume and building out the additional electrical grid infrastructure needed to deliver it” in order to ensure “that companies seeking to build AI data centers in Nevada don’t pass the costs of their increased energy usage to ratepayers.”
A spokesperson for Gov. Joe Lombardo echoed those points, saying Lombardo sees data centers as a part of Nevad’s economic growth strategy, but believes any “expansion or construction of data centers should not increase power rates for families or businesses, and impacts on the water supply must be carefully managed.”
Hill said Lombardo’s and Ford’s positions do not address the expansion of data centers with the urgency needed for impacted communities like Boulder City. Hill proposed establishing a new electric rate class to insulate residential and commercial customers from increasing demand.
“A stronger governor’s office is necessary to protect Nevadans from being taken advantage of by large corporations constructing new data centers,” Hill said. 
Representatives for NV Energy have told state legislators they believe Nevada will need 50% more energy than they projected needing just two years ago, and that energy demand could double by 2030. 
NVEnergy has acknowledged that the surge in demand will likely derail its ability to meet the state’s clean energy goals, which were placed in statute by lawmakers and then in the state constitution by voters.
Boulder City residents who attended the lively town hall were enthusiastic about the policies proposed by Hill, who thanked her for creating a town hall where their concerns could be heard. 
The issue has attracted enthusiastic opposition from residents of Boulder City, with more than 2,600 signing an online petition to stop the development. A scheduled hearing for the data center was also postponed a month after intense public outcry. 
Hill faces a campaign fundraising disadvantage in her Democratic primary race with Ford for the governor’s seat. Ford reported having $1.5 million as of Jan. 15, compared to Hill’s $306,000. Ford has also been endorsed by far more Democratic officials, including all five Democrats  in the state’s congressional delegation.

name: California
title: Can medical malpractice lawsuits protect LGBTQ youth from conversion therapy? This California lawmaker thinks so
description: Medical malpractice suits may be one way to stop therapists from using conversion therapy on LGBTQ youth.
text:
California lawmakers are advancing a new strategy to discourage efforts to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a Colorado law banning the practice. The strategy: Extend the statute of limitations for medical malpractice claims.
A bill introduced by Sen. Scott Wiener, a Democrat from San Francisco, would increase the time period during which someone could file a malpractice suit against a mental health professional for trying to change their sexual orientation or gender and harming them in the process. Depending on the age of the person who files the claim, the bill would increase the statute of limitations from three years to 22 years or within five years of discovering the harm.
“You can’t change someone who is LGBTQ into not being LGBTQ. All major medical associations agree that sexual orientation and gender identity are immutable characteristics, and that so-called conversion therapy is fraud that harms patients,” Wiener said during a recent Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.
Wiener likened the change to a similar move by the Legislature to extend the statute of limitations for victims of child sexual assault.
The committee voted 10-to-2 Tuesday to advance the legislation along party lines.
Major medical and mental health organizations condemn conversion therapy, which is rooted in the now-debunked theory that homosexuality was a mental illness. Studies link it to increased depression and suicidality — and no credible evidence shows it works.
California was the first state to ban using the practice on children in 2012, and many states followed suit. But last month, the Supreme Court sent a case contesting Colorado’s conversion therapy ban on First Amendment grounds back to the lower courts. In an 8-to-1 opinion, the justices sided with Kaley Chiles, a Christian therapist who argued the law violated her free speech rights because it allowed her to “affirm” a client’s sexual orientation but prevented her from speaking about changing their orientation for clients who have that goal.
The opinion did not rule directly on the constitutionality of Colorado’s conversion therapy ban, but Justice Neil Gorsuch implied in the majority opinion that Colorado’s ban would fail the “strict scrutiny” test required of laws that regulate speech.
“What this decision is essentially saying is that it doesn’t matter that states have an interest in regulating the quality of care for their patients. Her right to express herself doesn’t stop when she steps into her office and practices her profession that is licensed by the state” said Elana Redfield, an attorney and federal policy director at UCLA’s Williams Institute, which researches LGBTQ legal issues.
Making more time for malpractice claims
The decision endangers California’s law as well as dozens of similar laws in other states, but Shannon Minter, legal director for the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the court’s decision gives him some hope. Because almost all medical organizations have disavowed conversion therapy, attempting it would still be considered malpractice even if state bans are no longer in effect.
“After having some time to digest the opinion and read it carefully, it seems there is a very clear path forward, and at the end of the day paradoxically we’ll be in a much stronger legal position in terms of these protections,” Minter said.
In the majority opinion, Justice Gorsuch differentiated malpractice laws from bans stating that they allow “breathing room for protected speech.”
In California, a patient can sue a medical provider for damages if they believe they were injured by the provider’s negligent behavior. These types of cases require expert witnesses to testify about the accepted standard of medical care and also place the burden of proof on the patient.
The remaining obstacle, Minter said, is time. Many LGBTQ individuals don’t realize the harm until years later, well past the existing statute of limitations. Wiener’s proposal would solve that problem and help deter state-licensed therapists from engaging in the practice in the first place, he said. 
“One of the unique ways conversion therapy harms young people in particular is it encourages them to blame themselves for the therapy failing,” Minter said. “Almost (every time) that someone comes to us or another attorney realizing that it is not their fault, it’s too late. That has happened with us time and time again.”
Christian groups, parents oppose
Opponents of the measure say it’s a clear effort to circumvent the Supreme Court’s decision, which will likely prevent states like California from enforcing conversion therapy bans.
“If they can’t ban the counseling, they’ll bankrupt the counselors who do it,” said Greg Burt, vice president of the California Family Council, a Fresno-based Christian advocacy group.
Burt argued the Supreme Court was clear in ruling that a therapist’s speech during a client’s session is constitutionally protected and that Wiener’s measure, if passed, would face the same legal challenges since it would still effectively suppress speech.
Burt acknowledged that counseling is “pointless” if the client doesn’t agree with the goals of the therapy, but said some Christians may feel same-sex attraction or gender dysphoria but still want to live according to their faith.
“I would hope people can pick their own goals in counseling and it would protect anybody. Why is the government involved in which goals we have for our life regarding sexuality and gender identity,” Burt said.
The bill is also opposed by California Baptists for Biblical Values and other groups that have historically opposed state efforts to shore up protections for transgender youth.
Decision calls into question “talk therapy”
Julia Sadusky, a licensed psychologist in Colorado, co-authored an amicus brief in the Chiles v. Salazar case asking the Supreme Court to uphold the ban – and describes herself as a theologically orthodox Catholic. 
For years, she has counseled children from religious families who want to align their identities with their faith; the ban, she said, never got in the way of her work. She and another Christian psychologist developed a clinical method to help religious LGBTQ youth explore identity without coercive practices. 
The key distinction in her practice, Sadusky said, is that she never promises a predetermined outcome. Clients make their own choices about how to live — some pursue same-sex relationships, some do not, some transition, some don’t. 
“The focus is on, how do I resolve value conflicts that come up for me when I have conflicts between different aspects of my identity, not how do I change my identity as such,” Sadusky said.
She’s worried now that the Supreme Court’s decision will “wreak havoc on the credibility of therapy” as a clinical practice.
“The most troubling part to me was the framing of talk therapy as merely protected free speech, given that talk therapy incorporates treatment modalities or ought to, and isn’t merely telling a person what you believe about their life or what you recommend to them,” she said. 
Some legal scholars agree. Redfield with UCLA’s Williams Institute said the court’s decision could have widespread impacts on the medical field. 
“All patients should be concerned because this undermines our ability to trust doctors. And it places the burden on consumers to bring a lawsuit,” Redfield said.
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: California
title: State should probe L.A. County’s $4 billion sex abuse settlement
authors: Curtis Chambers and Regino Torres Jr.
description: LA County approved the deal without depositions or an independent review, resolving thousands of abuse claims in bulk. Employees couldn’t respond.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Curtis Chambers
Curtis Chambers is president of the Los Angeles County Deputy Probation Officers Union, AFSCME Local 685.


Regino Torres Jr.
Regino Torres Jr. is president of the Supervising Deputy Probation Officers Union, Teamsters Local 986.


LA County last year agreed to pay a record $4 billion to settle thousands of claimsof sexual abuse in county-run juvenile facilities and foster homes. Recently, nine people told the Los Angeles Times they were paid to sue, and one man said a false abuse claimwas filed without his consent. There are many perspectives on the controversy. This is from unions representing workers. One from a child advocate is here.
A recent report by The Los Angeles Times raised concerns about potentially false claims tied to Los Angeles County’s $4 billion sexual abuse settlement. It should serve as a wake-up call for state leaders.
This is not simply a local issue. 
Los Angeles County is a political subdivision of the state of California and receives substantial state funding to operate its juvenile and adult justice systems. When failures of this magnitude occur, the state not only has the authority to act, it has the responsibility.
AFSCME Local 685 and Teamsters Local 986 represent the probation officers and supervisors who carry out this work every day. These workers supervise youth, protect communities and operate in increasingly difficult conditions. 
They are also now dealing with the fallout of a settlement process that denied them the most basic element of fairness — the ability to defend themselves.
The county approved a $4 billion settlement without depositions, without evidentiary hearings and without a meaningful independent review. Thousands of claims were resolved in bulk, and the employees implicated were never given the opportunity to respond.
Now, with questions emerging about the legitimacy of some claims, the consequences of that approach are becoming clear.
Accountability matters. Survivors deserve justice. 
But justice requires a process that distinguishes between substantiated claims and those that are unverified or false. When that distinction is lost, public trust erodes and the state’s justice system is weakened.
The state cannot look away from this.
For years, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors has mismanaged the probation department through hiring freezes, chronic understaffing and policy decisions that weakened the workforce. Today, the department faces roughly 700 vacancies and a staffing shortage approaching 30%.
Even more troubling, the county has failed to build a sustainable workforce pipeline. In a recent hiring cycle, just 88 candidates were hired out of more than 8,500 applicants. Entry-level officers can wait up to a decade for promotion. 
At the same time, more than half the field workforce is nearing retirement age, and the county has refused to grant safety retirement, forcing officers to work longer than peers in other jurisdictions.
These are not isolated management issues. They are policy choices that directly impact the state’s ability to ensure safe and effective juvenile and community supervision systems.
The consequences are already evident. A court is now considering whether to place Los Angeles County’s juvenile division into receivership. That alone should trigger immediate concern in Sacramento.
The state has the tools and the obligation to act.
First, the California State Auditor should conduct a full forensic audit of the settlement process. Billions in taxpayer dollars, including funds that intersect with state-supported systems, were committed without sufficient transparency or verification.
Second, the Legislature should hold oversight hearings to examine how this settlement was negotiated and approved, and whether state funding streams are being used in a manner consistent with accountability and public safety.
Third, the state should condition future funding on measurable improvements in staffing, hiring, retention and operational stability. If the county cannot maintain a functional probation system, the state must require corrective action.
Finally, safeguards must be established to ensure that future large-scale claims processes include independent verification and basic due process protections. No public employee should be placed in this position again.
This is about more than one settlement. It is about whether California will ensure that its local partners operate systems that are fair, accountable and capable of delivering justice.
Los Angeles County’s failures are now affecting not only its workforce and its residents, but the integrity of the broader state system. The warning signs are clear.

name: California
title: California shouldn’t water down justice for these child sexual abuse survivors
description: LA County has pushed legislation that would set deadlines, limit damage and make it harder for sexually abused children in government care to sue.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Chantel Johnson
Chantel Johnson is a directing advocate at the Youth Law Center


LA County last year agreed to pay a record $4 billion to settle thousands of claimsof sexual abuse in county-run juvenile facilities and foster homes. There are many perspectives on the controversy. This is from a child advocate. Another perspective from unions representing the affected workers is here.
The recent revelation from 95-year-old Dolores Huerta that César Chávez sexually abused her decades ago is a stark reminder of what research has long shown: the ramifications of sexual abuse are profound and lifelong, and it often takes survivors decades to speak out about what they experienced when they were young.
But even as California legislators pledge support for Huerta and other survivors, they are preparing to introduce legislation that would block an entire class of sexual abuse survivors from ever seeking justice.
Last year, Los Angeles County reached a record $4 billion settlement with survivors of sexual abuse in its foster care and juvenile justice systems. New claims continue to pour in from survivors of abuse inside state systems.  
Now the county is pushing legislation that would create new deadlines, damage limits and immunity provisions, making it nearly impossible for those abused at the hands of the state to seek accountability. 
It’s a stunning betrayal for those who have already endured unimaginable harm.
For much of my own life, I have been connected to the foster care system in one way or another, first as a foster youth, later as a caregiver and now as a professional advocate.
Over the years, I have seen the very best of humanity in this system. I have watched foster parents, social workers, and advocates go the extra mile to comfort and care for children who have experienced unthinkable trauma. 
But I have also witnessed the very worst. I’ve seen children who were removed from their homes in the name of “protection” be abused again by the very systems meant to keep them safe. 
This new legislation would add to that trauma by denying survivors redress for harms that are well-documented and could have been prevented.
For generations, children placed in county-run facilities experienced widespread abuse, neglect, and exploitation. As far back as 1984, staff members at the notorious MacLaren Children’s Center were arrested on charges of child molestation, yet the abuse continued.
When the state takes custody of a child, it assumes one of the most fundamental responsibilities imaginable: keeping that child safe. L.A. County has failed to fulfill that most basic obligation.
Now, instead of confronting that failure honestly and fairly, policymakers want to change the rules by denying a particular subset of survivors the right to seek civil damages for the harm they suffered as children. 
County representatives are framing the proposal as a fiscal necessity in the face of California’s expanded statute of limitations for childhood sexual abuse, which brought a wave of claims against everyone, from the county to the Boy Scouts, to the Catholic Church. 
But the proposed law wouldn’t limit the rights of scouts or altar boys to seek damages for abuse they suffered as children. Instead, it singles out the disproportionately Black and brown youth who grew up in the custody of the county — a blatant attempt to balance the budget on the backs of the very children the government failed to protect.
The notion that young people who grow up in the care of public systems should have fewer rights than other survivors is outrageous. If anything, they should have more rights. No fiscal pressure justifies telling these young people that their suffering matters less or their rights are less valid than everyone else’s.
The forces that kept Huerta silent for decades can be overwhelming for youth in the foster care and juvenile justice systems who often lack stable adults, resources, or legal support. California recognized this reality when it expanded the statute of limitations. 
This new law would do just the opposite. It tells the public that when government institutions fail children, the solution is not reform, but immunity.
Worst of all, it tells survivors their trauma is less important than a balance sheet.

name: Nevada Current
title: Trump plans Nevada visit as prices skyrocket, consumer sentiment dives to record low
description: When Donald Trump comes to Nevada this week to celebrate “no tax on tips,” the venue will be packed with local MAGA faithful to cheer him on. Meanwhile, outside the room, the overwhelming majority of people throughout Nevada and the nation have a lot of feelings about Trump’s economy. Cheerful isn’t one of them. The […]
text:
Trump's most visible initiative to "lower prices" has been putting the words on a banner.(Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian)When Donald Trump comes to Nevada this week to celebrate “no tax on tips,” the venue will be packed with local MAGA faithful to cheer him on.
Meanwhile, outside the room, the overwhelming majority of people throughout Nevada and the nation have a lot of feelings about Trump’s economy. Cheerful isn’t one of them.
The monthly index of consumer sentiment conducted by the University of Michigan, based on phone interviews with hundreds of consumers nationwide and widely watched by economists and the business press, was released Friday.
U.S. consumer sentiment is at a record low.
At this point, a survey of consumer sentiment seems redundant. The same goes for the depressing inflation report that was also released Friday. Everybody knows what’s happening, and why.
Still, a record low is a record low. And a historical look at the index reveals the new record (“like nobody’s ever seen before,” to borrow Trump’s ubiquitous verbal tic) isn’t the only distinguishing feature about Trump’s impact on consumer sentiment. 
The causes underlying the economy’s ramshackle performance during Trump’s second term are also very unique, and very different from factors driving prior extreme dips in consumer confidence.
Consumer sentiment and the U.S. economy, 1952-2026
The University of Michigan national index of consumer sentiment was created in 1952. The index is normalized at “100,” and the higher the number, the more positive the consumer outlook.
Throughout the 1950s and 1960s the index pretty steadily hovered in the vicinity of 100, reflecting the post-World War II economic boom.
With the 1970s came oil shocks and stagflation. In late 1974 and early 1975, the index dipped below 60 for the very first time. 
Consumer sentiment rebounded for a few years, briefly edging above 90, until the Recession of 1980-82. That recession was triggered by a lot of things, including the Iranian Revolution of 1979 which intensified the energy crisis that had been bedeviling the economy throughout the 1970s. Consumer sentiment fell, and the index spent four months below 60 in 1980.
As the economy, or at least gross domestic product, emerged from that recession, consumer sentiment improved. In January, 1984, the consumer sentiment index edged above 100 for the first time since 1966, and would top 100 a couple more times that year.
With the exception of sluggish performance in 1990-92 (“It’s the economy, stupid,” as Bill Clinton’s campaign put it), consumer sentiment continued to improve, becoming downright exuberant (if irrationally so) in the late 1990s. In March 1997, the index once again topped 100. And it stayed above 100 every month but one for more than three and half years, until December 2000, recording an all-time high of 112 in January of that year. As no doubt Bill Clinton would be happy to tell you.
The economy in the 21st century could be described as a series of calamities (9-11, the Great Recession, the pandemic) followed by painful recoveries, and the index spent most of the first two decades of our current century below 90, often considerably below. One window of exception was Trump’s first term, when the nation was finally pulling out of the Great Recession. The monthly consumer sentiment index edged back above 100 five separate times during Trump’s first term.
The pandemic battered consumer outlooks, and the index fell below 60 through most of 2022 as the world struggled with inflation driven by supply chain chaos, a new oil shock as a result of Russian’s invasion of Ukraine, and federal policy that sought  — and succeeded — to stimulate an economic recovery that was quicker and more robust than anyone thought possible.
By the time Trump was inaugurated a second time in January 2025, the index had clawed back to 71.7.
That was the last time the index was higher than 70
Of the 16 full months Trump has been president, sentiment was in the 50s in 11 of them, including the last nine months straight. 
Even during the pandemic, as throughout the entire 74-year history of the University of Michigan index of consumer sentiment, the index never dropped below 50.
Until Friday. The preliminary survey results for April 2026 found a record low index of consumer sentiment of 47.6
A one-man show
To reiterate, a record low isn’t the only unique thing about Trump’s presidency with respect to the consumer sentiment index.
Shockingly high gas prices (and all the economic ripples that will follow from Trump’s war) weren’t the inevitable result of a combination of policies interacting with global developments and forces. The same goes for tariff-related inflation, or, for that matter, plummeting Canadian visits to Las Vegas.
Higher gas prices could extend into next year, says Trump administration energy agency

Unlike the energy crisis of the 1970s and early 1980s, the Great Recession, or the pandemic, the economic carnage that is crushing consumer sentiment now can be directly traced to the decisions made by a single individual. The record low consumer sentiment during Trump’s presidency is solely the result of decisions made by one person.
And what will that person say when he comes to Nevada this week?
According to his press secretary, Trump is coming to Nevada to tout what is one of the tiniest budgetary and economic provisions in his One Big Beautiful Bill. It’s a provision that has always been far more consequential as a political gimmick than it ever will be as an economic benefit for Nevada working households — a tax deduction, and a mere temporary one, with so many caveats and conditions that after filing their tax returns this year some workers say they feel they were “gaslit.”
Trump’s colossal blundering has brought nations on multiple continents to what increasingly resembles the brink of a world war. Even if he stumbles upon the holy grail in the form of the oft-invoked “off ramp,” the harm inflicted to the economy in Nevada, the nation, and the world will be deep and, by most projections, stubbornly persistent.
So not only faced with all that, but directly, personally, and, at bottom, solely responsible for it, naturally Trump is reacting by coming to Nevada to say “no tax on tips” to a friendly room.
A version of this commentary was originally published in the Daily Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: The terrible lows (and handful of peaks) in the 2026 Alabama Legislature
description: The Alabama Legislature has seemed discombobulated in recent years. It’s not just what happened on Thursday. The last day of a session is always frantic. Bills die without warning as a host of priorities try to squeeze through the closing door. But look at a controversial bill to require party registration to participate in Alabama […]
text:
(Left to right) Alabama House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainville; Alabama Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth and Alabama Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, preside over a joint session of the Alabama Legislature honoring veterans on March 19, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector) The Alabama Legislature has seemed discombobulated in recent years.
It’s not just what happened on Thursday. The last day of a session is always frantic. Bills die without warning as a host of priorities try to squeeze through the closing door.
But look at a controversial bill to require party registration to participate in Alabama primaries. This wasn’t one of those “controversial because it hurts Alabamians” bills. No, HB 541 divided the GOP. The state party wanted it. Many elected Republicans did not.
Managing that sort of legislation — whether you’re trying to pass it or kill it — takes a careful, coordinated strategy. As best as I can tell, Senate leadership Thursday put it on the calendar without any clear plan for handling it. They could have clotured Democrats to force it through. Or they could have let Democrats talk it to death. Instead, they did a little of both, cloturing Democrats but also jumping in and out of the calendar to avoid dealing with the bill.
The GOP caucuses in both chambers once got marching orders from leadership at the start of the session. A lawmaker disobeyed at their peril. Many grumbled about it. But the bills went through.
For better or worse, that’s not how things work anymore. Outside the budgets, the last four sessions have felt driven by individual legislators, lobbyists or whatever shiny object attracted the attention of conservatives.
The 2026 session continued the pattern. Some good bills came with a lot of awful ones, but there was never any sense of a grand strategy. Consider these lists representative, if not inclusive.
Positive developments
 
Breast and prostate screening: It shouldn’t be notable to see an Alabama lawmaker do something substantive about health care. But it is, and this was. Rep. Frances Holk-Jones, R-Foley, drawing on her own battle with breast cancer, pushed through legislation requiring insurers to cover secondary screenings — the exams that follow after a mammogram detects an abnormality. Similar legislation sponsored by Sen. Steve Livingston, R-Scottsboro, will do the same for prostate cancer.
It’s a crime that our nation forces many to choose between poor health or financial ruin. Anything that relieves the burden is a win.
Parole considerations: You know what a self-defeating criminal justice policy is? It’s telling the incarcerated that there is nothing they can do — no education, no rehabilitation — that can reduce their sentence. It discourages those in prison and puts corrections staff in danger. Hope maintains order.
And yet, for years this was Alabama corrections policy. The Alabama Board of Pardons and Paroles peevishly overlooked accomplishments to maintain punishment. Legislation from Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa will require board members to consider inmates’ attempts at improvement. Another bill sponsored by Sen. Sam Givhan, R-Huntsville will allow the board to use sanctions other than incarceration in case of parole violations, a response to a terrible incident last year where a man on parole who had rebuilt his life was sent back to prison.
Budgets: Alabama’s two budgets are tight, reflecting worries about the near-future of the state economy. But there are decent things in there, including modest pay raises for state employees and more money for health insurance (though not as much as state insurance boards sought). Another increases weights for populations covered under the RAISE Act, which gets more money for certain populations, including rural students, rural kids, kids in poverty and English language learners.

Better off dead

That closed primary bill: If I were a Republican legislator — especially one in Huntsville or the college towns — I’d be glad that HB 541 died. Giving GOP activists even more power over nominations is a surefire way to get even more extreme candidates. That’s not something the GOP can afford to do in rapidly growing places like Madison County.
Gun sales tax holiday: Taking the sales tax off firearms for a weekend would not impact the education budget much. But a state with one of the nation’s highest rates of gun violence does not need to make it easier to buy a firearm.
Archives changes: GOP lawmakers are still very angry that the Alabama Department of Archives and History hosted a program three years ago acknowledging the existence of LGBTQ+ Alabamians. So angry that they keep trying to make it a purely political board, obeying the conservative whim of the moment. Somehow, this manages to be both Orwellian and pathetic.
Immigration bills: We had a proposal to ban naturalized citizens from holding state office. Anti-democratic. Vicious. Elitist. And a really great message for a state that desperately needs immigrants to address workforce issues.
Right idea, wrong reasons
Grocery tax holiday: Alabama’s grocery tax is unusual, unfair and predatory. A grocery tax holiday, as outlined in a bill sponsored by Rep. James Lomax, R-Huntsville, and amended by Rep. Mike Shaw, R-Hoover, would give Alabamians a two-month respite from the tax. So what’s the problem?
The holiday takes place in May and June. Conveniently, those are also the months of the primary (May 19) and the primary runoff (June 16). After the elections, your tax returns. There’s a callous expediency to the bill that feels insulting.
Keep an eye on it
Blue Cross bill: I’m not convinced a bill letting Blue Cross Blue Shield reorganize itself as a nonprofit holding company is about “keeping jobs,” as Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, the sponsor of the bill, claimed on the floor of the Senate. Alabama may have many issues, but it has an endless need for health care workers.
A waste of time that will likely cost us
“Gulf of America:” Yes, southern Republicans must treat the word of Donald Trump as sacred revelation. But the Legislature’s approval of a bill designating the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” was a landmark in obsequiousness. Disrupting schools and agencies over a passing fancy the president had 15 months ago has no purpose. And when a more pro-geography administration comes in, we may have to change it.
A waste of money that will absolutely cost us
CHOOSE Act expansion: Legislators in their wisdom increased the funding for Alabama’s effective voucher program from $180 million to $250 million. This took place ahead of income-based eligibility caps coming off on Jan. 1. If you live in Alabama, congratulations: you’ll soon be paying the tuition of students enrolled at Indian Springs School in Pelham (tuition: $31,800 a year) or The Highlands School in Birmingham (tuition: $20,950 a year). And you have no choice.
The state’s education budget chairs argue that allocating a finite amount of money to the program will act as its own income cap. I’ll believe it when we have a budget year when legislators refuse to give the CHOOSE Act any more money.
The diabolical
Legislators v. nature: It feels like a long time ago, but the Alabama Legislature earlier this year voted to make it much harder for environmental regulators to address environmental problems in the state. The bill, sponsored by Sen. Donnie Chesteen, R-Geneva, prevents the Alabama Department of Environmental Management from adopting regulations stricter than the federal government and makes it next to impossible to pass new ones.
ADEM has suffered from underfunding and political interference for decades. But it should have the ability to act against polluters and protect the public. Legislators made that much more difficult.
Attacks on higher education: The Alabama Legislature’s war on colleges, the free exchange of ideas, and common decency continued with HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka. This bill would destroy professors’ abilities to represent themselves in faculty senates, turning them into catspaws for administration and making it far easier to fire instructors with tenure. It’s yet another step in turning Alabama’s colleges and universities into conservative re-education camps.
PSC Changes: Sometimes the Alabama Legislature lives down to its reputation. Faced with outrage over Alabama’s region-leading power bills, lawmakers from both parties knew what to do: Protect utilities from anything resembling accountability and stop the public from interfering.  You really don’t need much more proof to see that we live in an oligarchy, not a democracy.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Where the horses were tied outside
description: The state's horse racing industry generates billions in annual economic impact, provides jobs and preserves open space, write Alyse Cohen, but it needs help, particularly the off-track betting parlors like the one she operates, that have seen profits plummet.
text:
A rider slows in front of a flower display in this 2023 file photo from Pimlico Race Course. The track has since been tornd down and is being rebuilt, as the state's horse racing industry continues to grapple with ways to survive. (Photo by William F. Zorzi/Maryland Matters)My father took me to the Cracked Claw in Frederick, which was a seafood restaurant and also, in the way that Maryland places sometimes doubled as themselves, an off-track betting parlor. You could eat steamed crabs and watch a race happen somewhere else on a screen mounted above the bar.
It sounds improbable. It was completely ordinary. I understood, in the way children understand things before they can name them, that this was how a place held together, not by being one thing cleanly, but by accommodating the full range of what people actually wanted to do on a Tuesday evening.
That was August 1992, the year Gov. William Donald Schaefer legalized off-track betting. I didn’t know it was a big policy moment for Maryland, I only knew it as a place where my father and I sat together and watched horses run.
There is a quality to things that are genuinely local that is difficult to manufacture and easy to lose. It has to do with the way rural businesses and families in the same buildings carry memory. Frederick had that. The farms around it had that. The whole equine ecosystem of central Maryland also had it with the breeders, the farriers, the feed dealers and the trainers.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




What has happened since is not a tragedy exactly, but it is a change being discussed in certain ways before our General Assembly this year. Maryland now has 120 racing dates a year where it once had 175. The number of Maryland-bred foals — the next generation of the whole enterprise — has been cut nearly in half in three years. Pimlico, one of the most historic racetracks in the world, sat in rubble long enough that the State Sen. J.B. Jennings (R-Harford and Baltimore) said so plainly at a committee hearing, and no one disputed it.
The off-track betting parlors that were meant to extend the reach of racing have watched revenues fall so far that one operator reported earning $8,000 last year — for the entire year — on a facility the size of a small airplane hangar. He still owes the mortgage. I own an OTB today and it is down 38% in revenue year-over-year. The reason we went before lawmakers was that we’re worried our industry is dying.
There is something that deserves calling out loudly when a local industry is dying. Someone has to draw attention to it, because when businesses close, they do it too quietly. The shuttering doesn’t announce itself. It just goes. The horses are still there, the farms still there, the people who built their lives around this still there, and then one day the math stops working and the thing that was ordinary becomes memory.
In November, Gov. Wes Moore signed an executive order acknowledging what anyone who grew up around horses in this state already knew: the equine sector is not a relic. It generates $2.9 billion in annual economic impact. It employs an entire human ecosystem. It keeps open land open. The order called for a strategic plan, a coordinated future, a recognition that this industry is worth the deliberate effort of saving. The report is due in September 2026.
Senate Bill 639 is a less poetic than the executive order. It would have authorized wagering on historical horse races at licensed OTB facilities, capped at 4,000 terminals, overseen by the Gaming Commission, subject to a public referendum. It have would let the places that have survived — the OTBs, the small betting parlors, the rooms where people still gather to watch races on screens above the bar — compete for some portion of the $40 million in gaming revenue that currently crosses state lines every year because Maryland has given them no alternative product to offer.
Certain gaming businesses oppose it. This is understandable. It is also, when you look at it clearly, an argument that the machinery built to serve one part of Maryland’s life should be allowed to outlast the older life it displaced. I don’t think that’s what anyone intended. I think it is simply what happens when policy moves faster than the places policy is supposed to remember.
I grew up knowing that you could ride a horse to a roadhouse and tie it up outside while you went in and became briefly part of something larger than your own evening. That world is not entirely gone. But it requires, as all living things do, some conditions in which to continue. The legislature was asked to provide some of those conditions. I hope they remember what it felt like to be in a room where the horses were still tied up outside.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Why is CT bottle redemption up for debate again in 2026?
description: The bottle deposit rose to 10 cents two years ago. CT lawmakers are now questioning that move after the redemption rate rose to 97% in 2025.
text:
After years of seeing Connecticut’s bottle redemption rate dip below the 50% mark, lawmakers changed the deposit to 10 cents from 5 cents in 2024 to encourage more people to redeem their used bottles and cans.
Now that redemption rate sits at 97% in 2025 — meaning 97% of the bottles sold were returned in exchange for the deposit. But retailers and distributors argue that some of the increase in redemption rate might come from people traveling from neighboring states to redeem bottles not purchased in Connecticut, which would negate the purpose of the deposit and create revenue problems for them.
As a result, some legislators are now questioning whether the 10 cent program needs adjustment.
Here’s what to know.
Why does Connecticut have bottle redemption?
Oregon was the first state to introduce bottle redemption — at the rate of 5 cents in 1971 — with the goal of controlling litter from bottles and cans that ended up in the street. Nine other states have since added bottle bills, including Connecticut, which passed its 5 cent redemption bill in 1978.
That amount would equate to about 25 cents today if the deposit fee would have kept up with inflation, according to the Consumer Price Index’s inflation calculator, which it did not. Still, Connecticut residents received back $42 million from redemptions in 2023 alone.
Why the change to 10 cents?
Redemptions had been trending down in Connecticut for years, slumping south of 50% in 2020, despite a rate of well over 50% in the early 2010s. 
When Oregon, which had a similar problem, bumped its rate to 10 cents in 2017, the state saw its returns increase by over 15 percentage points in the following years.
So, in an effort to increase the number of bottles and cans recycled and cut down on litter, Connecticut lawmakers in 2021 voted to raise the redemption incentive to 10 cents as of Jan. 1, 2024.
Two years after increasing its own redemption amount, Connecticut’s rate jumped from 50% at the end of 2023 to 97% by the end of 2025.
Isn’t a 97% return rate a good thing?  
No, retailers and distributors argue. Retailers say that much of this increase is trucks from bordering states with low or no redemptions that have been traveling to their stores to redeem out-of-state bottles for cash in Connecticut.
And distributors say they have seen returns in certain parts of the state add up to more than the total number of bottles sold, and that out-of-state returns are to blame.
Under the current redemption system, retailers buy bottles for 10 cents from distributors and sell them to consumers with a 10 cent deposit fee. When consumers redeem their bottles, they get the money back from retailers and redemption centers, which in turn get 10 cents back from the distributor when they return the sorted bottles.



But distributors say they are spending more money redeeming bottles than they have been paid for. According to the state’s Department of Revenue Services, nearly 12% of wholesalers reported paying out more redemptions than they collected in deposits in 2025, totaling a loss of $11.3 million.
Any bottles consumers don’t redeem are considered forfeited. Distributors pay a portion of that cash to the state’s general fund and a portion to retailers and redemption centers as a fee (about 3 cents per bottle) that they use to operate their recycling rooms, and in some cases turn a profit.
What are lawmakers doing now? 
In the 2024 session, lawmakers made it illegal to knowingly redeem bottles from another state. And in 2025, they passed an emergency certification bill to crack down further, raising fines, allowing local police to go after out-of-state violators and requiring redemption centers to keep track of bulk drop-offs.
In 2026, two additional bills have passed to the Senate floor, one hoping to bring the incentive back down to 5¢ if the redemption rate exceeds 100% and the other to overhaul the system by putting the burden on distributors.
In a press conference on Wednesday, House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, said he did not want to see the redemption rate moved down to 5 cents this session.
“We’ll give it some time to see where it works its way through,” Ritter said.
Where do bottles go once they are redeemed? 
Once containers are sorted and cleaned, distributors funnel them into recycling streams. Aluminum cans are shredded into scrap metal and recycled into raw aluminum to be made into cans again. Glass is crushed and made into new containers or construction materials. PET plastic can be used in new bottles and packaging.
Single stream recycling can prevent contamination from other materials, increasing the quality of the recycled materials.
Connecticut has gradually been expanding the types of containers that are redeemable. In 2009, the legislature added bottled water to the existing list of soda and beer. And in 2021, the legislature included hard seltzers, hard ciders, juices, coffee and energy drinks.
Nips are currently not eligible for redemption, but consumers pay a 5-cent surcharge that goes towards environmental efforts in the town where they were purchased.

name: Mississippi Today
title: With the success of Sinners, the ‘Prince of the Delta Blues’ expands his kingdom
description: Keith Johnson performs with other musicians during Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience at Thalia Mara Hall in Jackson on Friday, March 27, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Throughout his life, Keith Johnson has heard fears of the death of the blues. 
Older Mississippi Delta blues musicians wondered if the genre would catch on with younger performers. They questioned whether younger local artists would be willing and able to perform the music.
